title: Religion and science
examples: Can science and religion both be true?
Was the Big Bang theory invented by a priest?
Why was Galileo put on trial?

b: Why is there a world at all?
What is life for, how should we live?

explain.say: Many people say science and religion often ask different kinds of questions. Science asks how the world works and tests its answers by experiment. Religions ask why there is a world at all, what life is for, and how we should live.

b: Why is there a world at all?

explain.say: Thinkers describe four main views of how the two relate. Some see conflict, some see two separate areas, some see a dialogue between them, and some try to fit them together into one picture.

draw.root: How do science and religion relate?
items: Conflict: they compete, one must win
Independence: separate questions
Dialogue: each can learn from the other
Integration: one combined picture

explain.say: History has famous clashes. In 1633 the Church put Galileo on trial for teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun. In 1859 Darwin's theory of evolution sparked debate that still continues for some believers today.

items: 1633: Galileo tried by the Roman Inquisition
1859: Darwin's On the Origin of Species
1925: the Scopes trial over teaching evolution
1927: Lemaître, a priest, proposes the expanding universe
1950 and 1996: popes say evolution can fit Catholic faith

explain.say: Yet many great scientists have been people of faith. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was a monk; Georges Lemaître, who first proposed what became the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest; and Abdus Salam, a Nobel Prize winning physicist, was a devout Muslim.

items: Scientist | Discovery | Faith
Ibn al-Haytham | Optics, how we see | Muslim
Isaac Newton | Gravity and motion | Christian
Gregor Mendel | Genetics | Catholic monk
Georges Lemaître | Expanding universe | Catholic priest
Abdus Salam | Unifying forces, Nobel 1979 | Muslim
Francis Collins | Human Genome Project | Christian

explain.say: Others see real tension. Some scientists, like Richard Dawkins, argue that science leaves no good reason to believe in God, while some believers read creation stories literally and reject evolution. Most believers today accept both science and their faith.

a: Some scientists: no need for God
b: Many believers: evolution is how God creates
Dalai Lama: Buddhism should change if science disproves it

explain.say: So can both be true? People give different answers, and that is a question you can think through yourself. A good start is to ask, for any claim, what kind of question it is answering.

items: What kind of question is it: how, or why?
What evidence could settle it?
Is a text being read literally or as a story with meaning?
Listen to scientists and believers fairly

faq.q: Can science and religion both be true?
faq.a: People disagree. Many believers and some scientists think they answer different questions, how the world works versus why it exists and what life means, so both can be true together. Others think they clash on some claims, such as miracles or the age of the Earth. It is a question you can weigh up yourself.
asks: do science and religion contradict each other
can you believe in God and science

faq.q: Why was Galileo put on trial?
faq.a: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried Galileo for teaching that the Earth moves around the Sun, which Church authorities then held to contradict scripture. He was made to take back his view and spent his last years under house arrest. In 1992 Pope John Paul II acknowledged that the Church had been wrong.

faq.q: Was the Big Bang theory invented by a priest?
faq.a: In a way, yes. In 1927 the Belgian Catholic priest and physicist Georges Lemaître proposed that the universe is expanding, and later that it began from a single primeval atom, the idea that became known as the Big Bang. Edwin Hubble's observations supported the expansion.
asks: who came up with the Big Bang
did a priest discover the Big Bang

faq.q: Does evolution mean there is no God?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Evolution explains how living things change over generations. Many believers, including the Catholic Church and many Protestant, Jewish and Muslim thinkers, see evolution as the way God creates, while some believers reject it and some atheists see it as removing the need for God.
asks: can you believe in evolution and God
what do religions think of evolution

faq.q: Are there scientists who believe in God?
faq.a: Yes, many. Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, was a monk; Georges Lemaître was a priest; Isaac Newton wrote a great deal about God; Abdus Salam was a devout Muslim and Nobel Prize winner; and Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project, is a Christian. Many other scientists are not religious.

It is an idea from the scientist Stephen Jay Gould, who was not religious. He argued that science and religion each teach with authority in their own area: science on facts about the natural world, religion on meaning and values, so they need not conflict. Critics say religions do make claims about the world.
asks: what did Stephen Jay Gould say about religion

faq.q: What did Islamic scholars add to science?
faq.a: In the Islamic golden age, roughly the 8th to 13th centuries, scholars in places like Baghdad made great advances. Al-Khwarizmi helped found algebra, and Ibn al-Haytham did pioneering experiments on light and vision. Many saw studying nature as a way of understanding God's creation.

faq.q: What do Buddhists think about science?
faq.a: Many Buddhists see their path as based on careful observation of the mind. The Dalai Lama has written that if science clearly disproves a Buddhist belief, Buddhism should change, and he has worked with scientists studying meditation.

faq.q: What do people mean by creationism?
faq.a: Creationism usually means reading scripture's creation accounts as literal science, for example that the Earth is only thousands of years old. Most scientists reject that, because of strong evidence that the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and many believers read the creation stories as meaningful but not literal.

faq.q: Can science prove or disprove God?
faq.a: Most scientists and philosophers say science studies the natural world by testing, so the question of a God beyond nature lies outside what experiments can settle. Some argue that scientific discoveries count as evidence for God, and others that they count against. That is why the debate continues.
asks: is there scientific proof of God

faq.a: In 1925 a teacher in Tennessee, John Scopes, was put on trial for teaching evolution, which a state law then banned. He was found guilty and fined, though the verdict was later overturned on a technicality. The trial became a famous symbol of the debate over evolution in schools.

faq.q: Is the conflict between science and religion a myth?
faq.a: Many historians now say the idea of constant warfare between science and religion, popular in the 19th century, is too simple. There were real clashes, like Galileo's trial, but also centuries in which religious scholars, monasteries and universities supported science.
asks: were religion and science always enemies

faq.q: What do non-religious people think about religion and science?
faq.a: Views vary. Some atheists, like Richard Dawkins, argue that science gives the best explanations and leaves no need for God. Others, like Stephen Jay Gould, thought science and religion could live side by side. Humanists usually rely on science and reason while valuing human meaning and ethics.
asks: what do atheists think about science
